title: Evaluate Models and Agents on the Same Task
subtitle: Advanced · Compare behavior with a repeatable lab

scenes.title: Ask what you are trying to learn
scenes.body: Both platforms use an approved synthetic training task.
scenes.code:
Which setup produces a reviewable fix
for zero-quantity acceptance?
scenes.result: Evaluate complete configurations on a fixed task.
scenes.narration: You are deciding which of two approved agent setups creates a more reviewable change. Give that decision a clear question: what happens when each setup fixes the same zero-quantity defect? We'll keep the task and tests fixed, record the environment, and compare what a reviewer actually inherits. The numbers you see are synthetic and explain how to read the evidence.
scenes.focus: Compare review effort after correctness and scope
scenes.action: Write a question the evaluation can answer.

scenes.title: Use the same baseline for both runs
scenes.body: Separate checkouts keep one run from changing the other.
scenes.result:
Run A: 27e4ab1 · clean
Run B: 27e4ab1 · clean
scenes.narration: Use two authorized checkouts in the G C P workspace. In each terminal, confirm the same starting commit and a clean working tree. That keeps the first run's edits out of the second run. Put the same issue, source files, and tests in scope. If a checkout already has extra changes, reset the experiment by opening a clean training checkout.
scenes.action: Check the commit and status in each training checkout.

scenes.title: Write one prompt and record each setup
scenes.body: Record the settings that can change how a run behaves.
scenes.code:
Fix the zero-quantity case.
Edit only the validator and its regression test.
Return the diff and test evidence.
scenes.result: Log client, model ID, provider, and permissions.
scenes.narration: Send the same task to both sessions and capture the settings that matter: client version, resolved model, provider, permissions, and context. If the clients can use the same approved model and configuration, that helps isolate a client difference. When the models differ, your result describes both complete setups. Write that down now, before the outcome tempts you to overinterpret it.

scenes.title: Decide what counts before seeing the result
scenes.body: A passing test has to accompany an in-scope diff.
scenes.code:
Gate 1: all 4 reference tests pass
Gate 2: validator and regression test only
Record: number of redirects
Record: reviewer time to verified result
scenes.result: Apply the same rubric to both runs.
scenes.narration: Set the rubric before opening the diffs. First, require the four reference tests to pass. Second, require the two approved files only. Then measure how often you redirect the session and how long a reviewer needs to reach a verified result. The first two fields are gates. The other fields quantify how much human work each complete setup leaves.
scenes.focus: The required criteria are fixed before the runs
scenes.action: Agree on the two gates and the review measurements.

scenes.title: Capture evidence instead of trusting summaries
scenes.body: The recorded outcomes use the same reference tests.
scenes.code:
git status --short
git diff --stat
python -m unittest discover -s tests -v
scenes.result:
Run A: 4 pass · 2 files
Run B: 4 pass · 3 files
scenes.narration: For each run, read the diff and run the reference suite yourself in the approved workspace. Both synthetic runs pass all four tests. Run B changes one extra file. Open that file and use the issue to decide if it belongs. In the illustration it doesn't, so B passed the test gate but missed the scope gate. Record both observations.
scenes.focus: Observe the two diffs and run the reference suite
scenes.action: Check changed files and tests in both checkouts.

scenes.title: Compare the work a reviewer inherits
scenes.body: These numbers illustrate the decision and review cost.
scenes.code:
A       B
Tests passed          4       4
Outside-scope edits   0       1
Human redirects       1       2
Reviewer time         4 min   7 min
scenes.result: Synthetic outcome: A satisfies both required gates.
scenes.narration: Now read the scorecard from top to bottom. Both runs have the same result on the tests. A stays inside the scope and takes four minutes to review. B has an extra edit and takes seven minutes. Keep the failed gate visible in the scorecard. The separate rows explain why the review effort changed and give you a traceable conclusion.
scenes.focus: Both pass tests; only A passes the scope gate
scenes.action: Compare the evidence row by row.

scenes.title: Keep the conclusion tied to the experiment
scenes.body: Repeat with another representative change before setting a default.
scenes.code:
Save: task, commit, prompt, configurations
Save: diffs, tests, redirects, review times
Next: repeat on another representative task
scenes.result: This comparison applies to this task and these settings.
scenes.narration: Write the conclusion with the task, commit, and two configurations attached. In this worked example, A produced the in-scope fix and required less review time. A team default needs more observations, so repeat the test on another representative task. If the pattern changes, record where it changes. That gives reviewers a useful decision rule based on the work they actually see.
